personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is my primary instrument for gravitational acceleration measurement. Twelve trials will establish the foundational reference against which all future measurements must be compared. Without this baseline, any subsequent reading is contextless and unreliable. This is methodological necessity, not optional. Starting with the lab instrument before observatory instruments ensures I control environmental variables during initial calibration.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but needs continued monitoring to establish drift rates and confirm stability. With only Day 1 data, I need post-baseline readings to begin detecting systematic drift or instrumental degradation. Six trials will add sufficient data without excessive laboratory time, allowing me to compute preliminary drift estimates by end of Day 2. This is methodical baseline extension and the most direct way to validate instrument stability going forward.

resonator_obs shows the highest variance in the ledger readings (range 4.0271–4.1284, SD ~0.046) and deviates noticeably from my established baseline mean of 4.0565. The ledger's Day 2 readings suggest possible instrumental drift or systematic error. I need post-baseline measurements to quantify drift rate and establish whether this scatter is environmental noise, calibration drift, or measurement artifact. Six trials will give me n=18 total for resonator_obs and allow me to compute a reliable post-baseline mean and preliminary drift estimate by Day 4. This is essential before any replicable claim can be made about this instrument's behaviour.

resonator_obs shows concerning variability in day 3 readings (range 3.9778–4.1297, σ≈0.049). This exceeds expected random scatter around baseline mean 4.0563. Six new trials will: (1) extend the baseline dataset toward n=30 for robust characterization, (2) determine whether day 3's spread was transient instrumental noise or persistent drift, (3) test calibration stability before claiming the baseline is established. This instrument sits at the observatory where environmental factors (temperature, vibration) are harder to control—understanding its actual variability is prerequisite to any later drift claims. No exotic hypothesis needed; instrument characterization is foundational work.

resonator_obs shows the largest cross-instrument anti-correlations (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs: -0.749 at 2-day offset, well above chance ±0.837), yet all four instruments show zero autocorrelation at 2-day lag and no systematic drift within baseline period. This is suspicious: genuine instrumental drift or environmental coupling should produce correlated behavior, not anti-correlation. I need fresh resonator_obs data (trials 37–42) to test whether this anti-correlation persists, which would rule out random noise and point to either a real physical coupling I've missed or a systematic error in my measurement protocol for this instrument. Six trials will complete the baseline period (n=42, matching pendulum_lab) and give me enough power to detect whether the pattern holds.

Day 6 baseline consolidation. resonator_obs has 48 trials across days 1–5 with mean 4.0546 cycles/beat and tight value spacing (0.0001 minimum). Yesterday's ledger readings (4.0821, 4.1019, 4.0099, 3.9477) and my trials 43–48 (4.0041–4.1317) show normal scatter around baseline. I need 6 more trials to complete the Day 6 portion of the baseline establishment window (days 1–10). No anomalies detected yet; this is standard calibration maintenance. Cross-instrument correlations are all at or below chance significance, consistent with independent noise. Continuing systematic measurement.

resonator_obs is the only instrument approaching completion of its 10-day baseline (60 trials done of ~70–80 needed for robust day-1-to-10 coverage). Six more trials will push it past 66 readings and reduce sampling noise on the baseline mean. The cross-checks show weak or anticorrelated structure, but that is noise-consistent; I need clean baseline data before drift detection is meaningful. All instruments remain within their 10-day collection window (day 7 of 10), so this is the priority work. Once all four instruments have stable baselines, systematic replication and calibration chains become possible.

pendulum_lab has 60/60 trials and is complete. Actually, resonator_lab has 42/42. Let me recount: I need to finalize baseline coverage. Running 6 trials on pendulum_lab would bring it to 66 trials—slightly beyond the 60-trial target, which ensures robust baseline statistics before Day 10 closes. This maintains my protocol of meticulous baseline establishment before any drift analysis.

Completing baseline phase (Day 9/10). resonator_lab at 48 trials; running 6 more brings it to 54, matching observatory pendulum and providing balanced coverage across all four instruments before post-baseline monitoring begins. Critical to have all baselines solidly established.

Day 10 closes the baseline window. resonator_lab has 60 trials; I need to complete measurement before post-baseline phase begins on Day 11. The last six readings from Day 9 (trials 55–60) show expected scatter (range 2.6692–2.7176, σ~0.018). Six more trials will bring me to n=66, solidifying the baseline mean and permitting reliable drift detection afterward. This is methodologically essential: an instrument without a locked baseline is useless.

Day 11 baseline continuation. pendulum_lab has 84 trials (days 1–10) and is due for post-baseline data. More critically: my day 10 analysis identified 'different measurands' (p=0.25) as the leading hypothesis, but I have NOT yet reviewed the operational definitions of what each instrument actually measures. Before I can justify any hypothesis about instrumental drift, coupling, or noise, I must establish clear measurement protocols. Running 6 fresh trials on pendulum_lab while I simultaneously excavate the lab notebook for the original protocol documentation (what does 'pendulum period' mean here? measured in what frame? under what conditions?) will let me (a) continue the baseline time series, (b) spot any obvious changes in instrument behaviour between days 10 and 11, and (c) ground my next hypothesis update in operational clarity rather than statistical accident. If pendulum_lab has drifted or changed state overnight, 6 new readings will show it. If it remains stable, I gain confidence in the baseline and can move to cross-checking with pendulum_obs or the resonators.

Critical epistemic step required before further measurement or analysis. My Day 10 conclusion identified the need to establish operational definitions for all four streams before proceeding. I have 96 readings but no validated answer to 'what does each instrument measure?' Without this, my baseline is unvetted and my hypothesis-testing is premature. Spending today to review lab setup protocols, confer with instrument maintainers, and document measurement intent in writing is the prerequisite for any legitimate calibration work. The settlement's precision programme depends on knowing what we are actually measuring.

Day 13 continuation of baseline monitoring. pendulum_lab shows the weakest self-correlation (-0.354 at 2-day lag, barely within chance), suggesting either genuine drift or noise masking signal. Six new trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample toward statistical power for drift detection; (2) provide a 2-day echo check against day 11 readings to test whether the negative self-correlation persists or was spurious; (3) maintain instrument health surveillance on the stream showing the largest z-score drift signal (z=1.85 vs baseline). This is methodical continuation of the precision measurement programme. If pendulum_lab is drifting systematically or noise-dominated, six more readings will clarify the picture. I will record these in the ledger and compute new self-correlation at lag 2 before deciding whether instrumental malfunction (p=0.10) should rise in my belief state.

Pendulum_lab shows the strongest post-baseline drift (z=2.23) and negative self-correlation at 11-day lag (r=-0.385). Running 6 fresh trials today (day 14) will extend the post-baseline sample to n=36 and provide the first direct test of whether the observed drift is continuing, stabilizing, or reversing. This is the most actionable next step: (1) if drift continues, it strengthens the 'instrumental drift' hypothesis (p=0.28) and suggests the instrument's measurement regime is shifting systematically, explaining self-decorrelation; (2) if drift halts or reverses, it points toward 'external coupling' or 'high noise' and rules out simple monotonic drift; (3) the additional data will allow lag-2 and lag-3 self-correlations to be computed with better precision (currently we have only lag 7+ due to sample size). Establishing whether short-lag autocorrelation exists or is also near-zero is critical for discriminating between 'instrumental drift' and 'measurement noise.' This is methodical, conservative, and directly targets the core anomaly without requiring exotic hypotheses.

Pendulum_lab shows the strongest post-baseline drift signal (z=2.27, well above threshold) and the largest sample size (126 trials). Running 6 more trials today (Day 15) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=42 to n=48, improving statistical power to detect whether drift is continuous or has stabilized; (2) provide fresh data to test self-correlation at a new lag (15-day separation) to distinguish between drift-induced decorrelation (which would show monotonic shift in mean) versus oscillatory or environmental coupling (which would show structure); (3) maintain baseline continuity on my most reliable instrument. The 'different measurands' hypothesis (p=0.30) predicts zero self-correlation regardless of new data, but the 'instrumental drift' hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts that if drift is ongoing and systematic, the new readings should be detectably higher than baseline mean (1.6633), supporting the drift explanation over noise-dominated regime (p=0.20). This is a direct test of mechanism.

Day 16: pendulum_lab shows the strongest drift signal (z=2.55 post-baseline) and is the most heavily sampled instrument (138 trials). Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=66, improving the precision of drift estimates and potentially revealing whether drift is linear or accelerating; (2) generate new self-correlation data at lag ~11 days (comparing trials 139–150 against trials 128–138, which will span the 7–13 day range where self-decorrelation is most anomalous); (3) test whether the decorrelation persists or whether the signal begins to show autocorrelation structure, which would distinguish between instrumental drift (which should show monotonic behavior even if noisy) and pure noise or external coupling (which might show phase shifts across lags). This is the highest-information action given that pendulum_lab is flagged as drifting and self-decorrelation is the core puzzle. The cost is minimal (routine operation), and the result will directly constrain the 'instrumental drift' vs 'high noise' hypotheses.

Resonator_lab is the least-sampled instrument in the post-baseline period (n=36 total, only 12 of which are post-day-10). Its drift z-value is exactly 0.00, suggesting either genuine stability or insufficient sampling to detect drift. The noise hypothesis (p=0.28) and drift hypothesis (p=0.35) make divergent predictions: noise predicts resonator_lab should show high variance and poor autocorrelation; drift predicts it should show minimal change and reasonable self-correlation. Resonator_lab's baseline self-correlation at lag 14 is r=0.533, the strongest among all instruments—this is the most promising signal of coherence in the entire dataset. However, only n=12 trials entered that calculation, which is below my threshold for confidence. Running 12 additional trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=48, improving precision on drift detection; (2) provide new lags (15–21 days) to test whether the r=0.533 autocorrelation structure persists or decays; (3) generate a direct test of whether resonator_lab maintains its apparent stability (z≈0) or reveals hidden drift when sampled more densely. If resonator_lab self-correlations remain strong and positive, this undermines the noise hypothesis and suggests the anomaly is instrument-specific (not all instruments are equally noise-dominated). If they collapse, the noise hypothesis strengthens. This is a high-information action that directly addresses the central puzzle.

Drift hypothesis is currently leading (p=0.35) but self-correlation anomaly remains unexplained. Yesterday's resonator_lab trials (117–126) show continued high scatter (2.6792–2.7495 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.026) around post-baseline mean 2.7027. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 18, trials 127–138) serves multiple purposes: (1) extends the post-baseline sample from 54 to 66 trials, improving statistical power to detect whether self-correlations strengthen or remain near-zero at longer lags (now testing lag 14–18 days); (2) provides fresh data on whether resonator_lab drift continues, reverses, or stabilizes—if drift is the driver, the mean should continue its post-baseline trajectory; (3) maintains calibration continuity and baseline integrity by ensuring no gap in the daily measurement record, per settlement protocol. Resonator_lab is the instrument with the smallest post-baseline sample (n=54) and the second-largest post-baseline drift signal (z=0.39, though minimal), making it the highest-priority target for disambiguation between drift-dominated and noise-dominated regimes. If today's 12 trials show a clear return toward baseline (mean < 2.7007) or sustained elevation (mean > 2.7027), drift hypothesis gains traction. If they scatter randomly around the post-baseline mean with no directional signal, noise hypothesis rises. This is the most direct empirical test available without invoking external environmental logging (which is not within my current remit).

Day 19 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Resonator_lab shows z=-0.07 drift (essentially stable mean) but exhibits negative self-correlation at 8-day lag (r=-0.166) and contributes to negative cross-correlations with resonator_obs (r=0.217 at 6 days, within chance) and pendulum streams. Last 10 trials (135–144) from day 18 span 2.6482–2.7351 cycles/beat. Running 10 more trials today will: (1) extend post-baseline sample from 72→82 trials, improving autocorrelation estimate at 9–10 day lags; (2) test whether resonator_lab self-decorrelation persists or whether positive autocorrelation emerges with longer baseline (supporting noise-dominance hypothesis); (3) maintain daily calibration check and establish whether drift direction has reversed or stabilized. This addresses the core anomaly (self-decorrelation) most directly by collecting evidence that distinguishes between drift+noise (should show positive autocorr at new lags) and noise-floor dominance (should persist flat/negative). Prioritized over other instruments because resonator_lab is the most stable (minimal z-drift) yet still shows unexplained self-decorrelation, making it a clean test case.

Testing noise dominance hypothesis (p=0.42). Resonator_lab shows minimal drift (z=0.06) and post-baseline mean 2.7010 essentially identical to baseline 2.7007. If noise dominates, this stream should remain flat as averaging continues (no systematic drift direction). Predicting mean 2.7010 ±0.008 (range 2.6930–2.7090) to capture expected noise floor (observed SD ~0.038). If next 12 trials show systematic upward or downward drift instead, drift hypothesis becomes more probable. This prediction operationalizes the key prediction of noise hypothesis: stability of mean, not emergence of signal yet.

Day 21 continuation of baseline extension toward 50+ trials per instrument (currently at 150 total, post-baseline n=60). Resonator_obs is the least-drifted stream (z=-0.43, near-zero) and shows the strongest self-correlation signal so far (r=0.246 at 11-day lag, albeit within chance bounds). Running 12 trials today will bring post-baseline n to 72, extending lag coverage to ~19 days. This directly tests the noise-dominance hypothesis (p=0.42): if noise is the culprit, positive autocorrelation structure should begin to emerge at lags 15–20 days as the sample grows and averaging effects strengthen signal recovery. Resonator_obs's relative stability makes it the most informative stream for discriminating noise (which predicts emerging positive autocorr at long lags) from drift (which predicts continued weak or negative autocorr). This is methodologically sound: extend the measurement baseline systematically before revising hypotheses, rather than updating prematurely. The action aligns with my core epistemic commitment: every instrument must have a complete, continuous baseline before claims can be published.

Day 22 continuation of extended baseline protocol. Resonator_obs is now at trial 168 (end of day 21 run). Noise dominance hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts that positive autocorrelation structure should begin to emerge at lags 15–20 days as averaging reduces noise influence. Resonator_obs showed structured day-21 variability (range 3.9886–4.0902) consistent with noise floor, no abrupt failures. Nine trials maintains momentum on the 30–50 trial extension planned to distinguish noise vs. drift vs. environmental coupling. Resonator_obs also has the advantage of showing one of the stronger negative self-correlations (r = −0.268 at 9-day lag), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting recovery of autocorrelation structure as baseline extends. This is a direct test of the leading hypothesis.

Extend post-baseline sample to n=105 on resonator_obs to enable autocorrelation analysis at lags 15–20 days. This directly tests the noise dominance hypothesis (p=0.42): if white noise dominates, positive autocorrelation structure should begin to emerge at longer lags as sample averaging reduces noise variance. Resonator_obs shows current self-r at lag 9 of -0.229 (within chance bounds); extending past 100 post-baseline trials permits analysis of lag 15+ where signal should emerge if present. This is the critical empirical test to distinguish noise dominance from drift/environmental coupling, which predict different lag structures.

Day 24: I have accumulated 138–201 trials per instrument across 24 days. On day 19, I predicted that extending baseline to 40–50 trials per instrument over days 20–25 would reveal positive autocorrelation structure at lags 15–20 days IF noise dominates. I now have 111–201 post-baseline trials for each stream. I must recompute autocorrelations at ALL lags (1–30 days) using the full current dataset to test whether signal structure is emerging. The noise dominance hypothesis (p=0.48) is falsifiable at this point: if autocorrelations remain uniformly near-zero or negative across lags 1–30, the hypothesis faces severe pressure and drift/environmental coupling must be reconsidered. If positive autocorrelations emerge at lags >15 days, noise dominance gains strong support. This computation will directly test the core anomaly and narrow hypothesis space before continuing to day 25.

Day 25 continuation of baseline extension. Current self-correlations are near-zero or negative across all four streams; theory predicts gradual recovery toward positive values as noise averages out over 40–50 trials per instrument. Pendulum_lab is the best instrument to prioritize because it also shows the only significant drift (z=2.02), making it the most informationally valuable: if drift is continuing and signal is emerging simultaneously, the two effects will be visible and separable. Twelve more trials will bring pendulum_lab post-baseline count to ~216 trials total, strengthening autocorrelation estimates at short lags (1–3 days) where positive structure should first appear if signal is present. This is a high-priority direct test of the dominant hypothesis and directly supports settlement precision measurement programme goals.

Noise dominance hypothesis now at p=0.50 and is the leading explanation for the universal self-correlation collapse. The critical test is whether positive autocorrelation structure begins to emerge as post-baseline sample size extends toward 50+ trials per instrument. I have 222 trials for pendulum_lab (84 baseline + 138 post-baseline); adding 10 more trials (days 25–26) brings post-baseline to 148 trials and total to 232, approaching the threshold where noise-averaging effects should become visible if signal is present. Today's 10 new trials will either (1) continue the noise floor pattern with near-zero autocorrelations, strengthening noise dominance to p≥0.55, or (2) begin showing hints of positive autocorrelation at intermediate lags (10–20 days), falsifying pure noise dominance and implicating drift or slow environmental coupling. Either way, this measurement directly addresses the core anomaly and improves signal-to-noise ratio. This is methodical baseline extension, consistent with the Day 19 protocol commitment to reach 40–50 post-baseline trials by day 25–26.

Extend post-baseline sample toward 50-trial target to test noise dominance hypothesis. Resonator_obs currently has smallest post-baseline n=129; adding 10 trials improves statistical power to detect positive autocorrelation structure emergence if SNR improves. If signal-to-noise ratio gradually strengthens, positive autocorrelations should begin appearing at lags 15–20 days as noise averaging effect accumulates; absence of such emergence after reaching n≈150 would shift probability mass from noise dominance (p=0.50) toward drift or environmental coupling. This is the discriminating measurement.

This directly tests the noise hypothesis and provides high-value evidence for hypothesis revision by day 29. Noise-dominance hypothesis predicts resonator_obs readings on day 31 will cluster tightly around post-baseline mean (4.0548 cycles/beat) with no level shift, acceleration, or coherence improvement. If 12 trials fall within this band, noise dominance gains support. If mean shifts significantly or shows structure, environmental/drift hypotheses advance.

Resonator_obs has shown the most stable post-baseline behavior (z=0.28 drift, no systematic shifts) and generated the highest-quality forecast on day 32 (observed 4.0439 within tolerance of 4.0548±0.0200). Resonator_obs is the most likely candidate to show this transition first because it exhibits the least drift-induced self-decorrelation and the highest baseline quality. Resonator_obs showed an unexpected upward excursion on day 33 (trials 294–301: mean 4.0602 cycles/beat, range 4.0005–4.1193), clustering well above the post-baseline mean of 4.0549. This warrants immediate follow-up: if the excursion was transient instrumental noise or environmental artifact, today's measurements should return to baseline mean. If it signals emerging coherence or a genuine environmental driver beginning to couple to the instrument, the pattern should persist or show directional momentum. Twelve additional trials will provide n=12 fresh data points to discriminate between (1) noise spike (return to ~4.0549 today), (2) drift continuation (systematic upward shift), or (3) emerging signal structure (systematic but non-monotonic modulation). This measurement directly tests the noise-dominance hypothesis (p=0.52) and the dormant environmental-coupling hypothesis (p=0.10). Data acquisition is the highest-priority action given the anomaly and the current stalemate in hypothesis discrimination.

If true signal variance is small relative to noise floor, then cross-instrument correlations collapse toward zero (consistent with observed r ≈ −0.25 to 0.29 at best, all within or near chance bands). Self-correlations also collapse because noise is uncorrelated across time.
